KEY MESSAGE 1...Hot and very humid conditions are expected to 
persist through Tuesday of next week. A Heat Advisory is in 
effect for portions of the area.

A relatively stagnant synoptic pattern is developing across our
region. Quasi zonal mid and upper level flow will be in place 
through the middle of next week as Bermuda high pressure 
persists offshore. This will keep a steady stream of very warm 
and moist air in place across the region through the period.

A prolonged period of hot and, most notably, very humid 
conditions is expected to remain in place for the next several 
days. We look to have a weak cold frontal passage early Sunday, 
ushering in slightly drier air. This will give some slight 
reprieve from the excessive humidity, though highs will still be
in the upper 80s to low 90s. Moisture advection will return 
again by Monday though, and hot and very humid conditions are 
anticipated to return Monday through Tuesday. A somewhat 
stronger cold front looks to come through late Tuesday or 
Wednesday, which will help break the excessive heat and humidity
some.

A Heat Advisory remains in effect for portions of eastern 
Pennsylvania, much of New Jersey except the far southern 
counties, as well as New Castle County, Delware. A portion of 
the Heat Advisory for northern New Jersey and southeastern 
Pennsylvania was extended through Saturday. This includes Morris
and Hunterdon Counties in NJ, and upper Bucks, western
Montgomery, and western Chester Counties in PA.


KEY MESSAGE 2...There are daily chances for showers and 
thunderstorms through Saturday, as well as much of next week. 
There is at least a marginal risk each day for localized heavy 
rainfall leading to flash flooding and locally damaging wind 
gusts with any stronger thunderstorms that develop.

Diurnally driven instability will mostly be in the 1000-2000 
J/kg each afternoon through the next several days (except for
Sunday) along with PWats in the 1.5-2" range. Mean flow will be
predominantly southwesterly and relatively weak through 
Saturday. This will support a continued localized heavy rainfall
threat with potential for flash flooding, although water loaded
downdrafts could cause localized wind damage. Areas with very 
saturated ground from recent rains will be most prone to 
experiencing trees falling.

For late this afternoon and evening, a mid level shortwave 
trough will approach the area, providing more forcing (as 
compared to Thursday). As such, storm coverage is expected to 
be more widespread, and storms should be more organized, 
although bulk shear values are still relatively modest (up to 25
kts). Latest environmental parameters and CAMs indicate we
should see some scattered thunderstorms developing across
eastern PA by mid afternoon. Given the weak low level shear, 
cold pool development should begin to propagate eastward fairly
quickly. This should ultimately support an MCS or two of sorts 
developing and moving toward the I-95 corridor ahead of maximum
boundary layer thermodynamics. This will support damaging wind
gusts for a couple hours or so as this MCS(s) moves east.
Exactly where the greatest severe threat will be will depend on
where the early activity begins developing upstream. As the
activity moves east, a loss of diurnal heating and accelerating
cold pool cutting off inflow should cause storms to weaken 
toward the coast. Forward motion of the storms should preclude a
significant flash flood threat, so we have not issued a Flood
Watch, however PWats of 2-2.25" will support very heavy rainfall
rates of 2-3" per hour. If these were to impact urbanized areas
for long enough, there could certainly be some flash flooding 
concerns.

All of that said, the threat of severe thunderstorms today has
increased, and SPC has add a Slight Risk for damaging winds
along and northwest of I-95 (Marginal Risk elsewhere in the
forecast area). We remain in a Marginal Risk for excessive
rainfall from WPC.

Details for Saturday's convection remain unclear, but we could 
certainly end up with some potential for flash flooding and 
severe storms again. Current indications in the guidance support
a later timing of storms during the evening or even overnight 
depending on the timing of a weak cold front and shortwave 
trough. PWats look slightly lower than today, and mean flow is a
bit more westerly than southwesterly, but overall the 
thermodynamics appear similar. There will be less forcing, so 
convection probably won't be as widespread as today. We remain 
in a Marginal Risk for excessive rainfall from WPC and general 
thunder from SPC for Saturday.

We look to have a weak cold frontal passage by early Sunday, 
ushering in slightly drier air. This combined with subtle 
subsidence aloft will help briefly limit convection potential on
Sunday and also give some slight reprieve from the excessive 
humidity, though highs will still be in the upper 80s to low
